Engineering performance study · Field report 01 · Revised edition

Qwen Next on
Strix Halo & Blackwell

Single-host inference, native multi-token prediction, and a two-machine GPU experiment. A reproducible account of the configurations that completed, the ones that did not, and what the evidence can establish.

Record date: 17 November 2026 · Prepared for Scott · Report version 2.0
One base model: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next GSQ-RCO / IQ3_S · 13 selected configurations · 72 requests · 8 figures
FindingsModelMethodsEngine comparisonNative MTPLatencyCalibrationTwo GPUsResourcesValidityAll measurementsEvidence

01 / FindingsWhat the completed tests show

The tested llama.cpp candidate ran the large Qwen Next model on all three machines. Strata delivered higher decode throughput in every selected, matched-workload engine comparison with drafting disabled. Native MTP reduced throughput in both completed native off/on comparisons. The two-host RPC run completed one coding answer, much more slowly than either single GPU.

-7.67%Native MTP change on the 5060 Ti at 24,842 input tokens: 4.486 → 4.141 tokens/s. A decrease; the denominator is MTP off.
4.04×5070 Ti Strata/native decode-rate ratio at 24,842 input tokens, both MTP off. 21.00 versus 5.19 tokens/s.
12.45×More decode time per token for the tested two-GPU route versus the 5070 Ti native single-GPU run, on a byte-identical 169-token coding answer.
Scope of the conclusion. These are observed configuration comparisons, not an estimate of every engine's best possible performance. Cache budgets, auxiliary layouts and some runtime settings differed. Each cell is one execution; no confidence intervals or statistical significance claims are warranted. The original benchmark evidence is reused. No inference was performed to produce this report.

Measured: model identity, engine timing, request latency, answer hashes, resource observations and saved correctness receipts. Inferred: remote expert transfers and serial dependencies are plausible contributors to RPC overhead. Not measured: a direct peer-to-peer RPC baseline, isolated SSD bandwidth, power efficiency, universal coding ability, or optimal settings for each backend.

Workload and sequence

  1. One server slot, context 32,768, 16 threads, flash attention, temperature zero, thinking disabled, streaming, output cap 256, and prompt-cache reuse disabled for the native request protocol. Native KV cache was q8_0. Strata used its int8 KV setting; bitwise equivalence is not established.
  2. A short warmup preceded full suites. Then three serial short-code requests used the same task with trial markers #trial0, #trial1, and #trial2. These are sequence positions, not independent replications. The selected Halo 32 GiB cache comparison retains five task requests per condition without an included warmup row.
  3. Long cases added 300 or 1,200 structured records containing warehouse item, quantity and region fields, producing 6,123 and 24,842 measured prompt tokens. Every task asked for the same function. There was no randomized order or controlled cold OS-cache reset.
  4. Timing comes from engine response timing records and client wall-clock/first-token measurements. Decode TPS is retained as reported by each engine; timed-token conventions can exclude a first output token. It is not reconstructed as output count divided by duration.

The Blackwell native cache was 6 GiB, while Strata chose approximately 7.94–9.12 GiB. Halo Strata used 44.63 GiB, versus 32 GiB for the native cached MTP pair. H-GPU is a GPU-offload baseline with lazy per-layer embeddings, not a claim that all 77.88 GiB resided on the GPU. Blackwell native working-set caps began at 8 GiB and were raised to 18 GiB before the measured protocol; Strata used 12 GiB. Native MTP allowed up to three draft tokens with minimum probability 0.5; Strata allowed four at 0.5. Native draft microbatch was 128 on Halo and 512 on the 5060 Ti.

Native cached conditions used memory-mapped experts, CPU expert share zero, disabled automatic fitting and disabled the extra RAM cache. Blackwell native CUDA children used the supported GGML_CUDA_NO_PINNED=1 environment override after pinned-host loading exceeded headroom. This affected only the isolated benchmark children; no global environment or Windows setting changed. The source harness, native logs and approved guard boundary receipts are registered below. Exact argument lists are in section 11.

Definitions and denominators

MTP throughput change (%) = 100 × (TPS_on / TPS_off − 1)
Normalized token-time change (%) = 100 × (TPS_off / TPS_on − 1)
Strata/native rate ratio = TPS_Strata_off / TPS_native_off
Native below Strata (%) = 100 × (1 − TPS_native_off / TPS_Strata_off)
Observed wall change (%) = 100 × (wall_on / wall_off − 1)

A 50% rate decrease means twice the time per token, not 50% more time. Request wall time additionally depends on prompt processing and answer length. No cross-workload average is used as a headline result.

05 / Native draftingMTP slowed both completed native comparisons

On the 5060 Ti, native MTP reduced decode throughput by 6.84% to 18.20% across the five workloads. At 24,842 prompt tokens it fell from 4.486 to 4.141 tokens/s: a 7.67% rate reduction, equivalent to 8.31% more generation time per token. Request wall time rose 4.76%, but the generated answer also grew from 163 to 198 tokens.

The 6,123-token 5060 Ti pair is a stronger answer-controlled comparison: both responses were byte-identical and 123 tokens long. MTP still reduced decode throughput by 6.84% and increased client wall time by 2.55%. The other pairs are valid observations of serving behavior, with an additional answer-length/content confounder.

The selected Halo 32 GiB cache pair also lost throughput on every task. This does not establish that all native MTP implementations or settings are slower. It establishes that these auxiliary weights, draft settings and hardware did not recover their extra work through sufficient accepted draft tokens. Acceptance counters support inspecting that tradeoff; a dedicated kernel-level cost profile was not collected.

06 / Latency & orderingA faster decode rate need not mean a faster request

The stacked bars are engine prompt and generation intervals. The labels show independently measured client wall time and output length. Small differences between their sum and wall time arise from timer boundaries, setup and streaming overhead; they are not allocated to a measured “network overhead” component. Some records differ by a few milliseconds in the other direction.

For example, on the 5060 Ti at 24K input, Strata MTP decoded faster than Strata off (19.9 versus 18.7 tokens/s), yet observed wall time increased from about 164.33 to 166.17 seconds. Prompt processing dominates that request and the responses need not be equally long. Selecting only decode TPS would miss the user-visible outcome.

These three short coding positions follow one another within a live server. Warm expert caches, prompt markers and response variation can affect them. Connecting the points displays their ordering; it is not a fitted trend, independent replication, or an uncertainty interval.

08 / Two-host experimentMore capacity, but serial work across a relay

The two cards remained separate devices on separate computers. The test partitioned one model's layers across them using llama.cpp RPC. It did not create one physically unified 32 GB GPU, and it did not turn each generated token into two independent jobs.

5070 TiNative coordinator + local CUDA GPU
→
Halo relaySSH remote forward → SSH local forward
Tailscale on both legs
→
5060 TiLoopback RPC service, port 50052
Remote CUDA GPU

This relay topology was a test setup choice. There is no direct 5070↔5060 RPC control in the evidence, so the experiment cannot assign a precise fraction of the slowdown to llama.cpp, the physical network, encryption, the relay, storage, or expert-cache misses.

What explains the result—and what remains unresolved

  • Demonstrated capacity: GPU expert caches were 9,209.25 and 9,205.10 MiB; associated model buffers were 1,822.94 and 2,160.06 MiB. Approximately 21.87 GiB of combined weights/cache allocation exceeded either card alone. That allocation does not prove that every cache slot held a useful expert. Sampled total GPU use was 13,704 and 13,677 MiB, including KV, compute, runtime and desktop allocations.
  • Network traffic was real: across a 122.72-second whole-Halo adapter observation, Tailscale received/sent approximately 18.89/18.89 MiB/s; Ethernet approximately 21.36/21.17 MiB/s. [E048] These are adapter-wide counters, not isolated RPC payload rates or a saturation test. An earlier ~1 ms discovery ping is not a measurement of expert-transfer latency.
  • Mechanism consistent with the observation: CPU share was zero; expert misses therefore needed GPU upload rather than local CPU expert computation. The captured source's src/llama-moe-cache.cpp upload path calls backend tensor transfer, which becomes a network transfer for a remote backend. Layer dependencies and autoregressive token generation introduce serial waits. GPU samples were often idle, consistent with waiting rather than continuous compute saturation.
  • Memory guard was not the cause of this completed answer's slow decode: the RPC coding interval retained roughly 8 GiB of free host RAM, above the restored 5 GiB inference floor. The run was intentionally stopped after one validated answer to try CPU participation; it did not complete a long-context suite.
  • Alternatives did not produce benchmark results: CPU share 0.95 stopped during loading at the hard memory floor. A separate resident split configuration allocated approximately 22.26 GiB of GPU model buffers but demanded about 29,472 MiB of anonymous CPU memory and stopped before answering. Neither is evidence of successful faster serving.
Plain-English conclusion: the second card added storage space for model data. Each token still had to wait for the appropriate machine and transfers. This particular relay and cache configuration made those waits expensive. The experiment establishes the outcome, but it does not establish an unavoidable speed limit for all distributed llama.cpp deployments.

09 / Resource behaviorWhat the memory and disk observations mean

The traces compare whole jobs on the 5070 Ti, including startup, using each job's own elapsed time. Native off and Strata MTP are different configurations and took different lengths of time. Cumulative disk counters are system-wide. Sampled GPU utilization is sparse; it is not a synchronized GPU profiler.

Windows page-fault totals combine soft and hard faults. They cannot be relabeled as SSD reads or disk faults. Strata's engine runs as a child process; inspecting only its Python launcher would undercount its memory and fault activity. These observations demonstrate substantial storage/memory interaction, but do not isolate peak SSD capability or prove one drive is the bottleneck.

10 / Correctness, exclusions & validityThe limits belong beside the results

61 selected coding answers; 90 archive receipts

There are 72 requests in the selected dataset: 11 warmups and 61 coding answers. Each selected coding answer was matched to an existing validation receipt by result filename, workload label and SHA-256; all 61 passed the ten recorded independent input cases for this task. [E014] The wider archive contains 90 passing receipts because it also includes 29 older or supplementary answers outside these selected configurations. Reporting 90 as the selected study's answer count would be incorrect.

This verifies basic behavior for stable_unique and its recorded test cases. It does not establish repository-scale coding quality, agent reliability, tool-use capability or general model superiority. No additional code generation or inference was used to improve this result.

Threats to validity

  1. Single execution per cell. The three short positions differ by markers and cache history. No randomized repeats, confidence bounds, p-values or independent cold-start variance estimates are available.
  2. Unequal cache and runtime settings. Strata chose larger Blackwell caches and a different host working-set cap. Halo cache comparisons use different budgets. These are deployment comparisons, not an isolated backend algorithm experiment.
  3. Answer variation. Temperature zero does not guarantee bitwise equivalence across kernels, engines or drafting. Hashes identify the stronger answer-controlled pairs. Most request-latency comparisons include different response lengths.
  4. Machine differences. CPU, RAM speed, drive and driver differ. The two Blackwell hosts are not a controlled GPU-only A/B test.
  5. Drafting differences. Native and Strata auxiliary layouts, vocabulary, maximum draft lengths and normalization differ. No all-else-equal claim is made across their MTP conditions.
  6. Storage/cache history. Windows memory-mapped files, standby cache, prefetching and a live desktop make cold-storage behavior uncontrolled. A working-set cap is not a complete bound on system-wide prefetch pressure.
  7. RPC route and sample size. Two SSH/Tailscale legs via Halo, zero CPU expert share and one completed code answer leave multiple causal contributors unresolved.
  8. Task diversity and timing conventions. One simple Python task with filler contexts is not a broad coding benchmark. Engine timing conventions differ; client latency is reported separately.

Preservation and safety cutoff

The recorded loading-only exception stopped immediately below 2 GiB free physical RAM or 4 GiB free commit, and allowed at most ten seconds below 5 GiB physical RAM during loading. The original 5 GiB physical / 4 GiB commit inference threshold was restored before inference. This was the explicitly approved loading exception; Windows settings were not relaxed.

Historical completion receipts record owned model/RPC/SSH processes stopped, remote GPUs back near their baseline allocations (approximately 401/392 MiB), serving-profile identity preserved and model file size/time metadata unchanged. [E053] [E054] [E055] The final preservation check did not rehash the full 83.6 GB base model; original SHA receipts and final metadata are different evidence tiers. These statements describe the saved experiment cutoff, not a new live machine-status assertion when this report is opened later.

12 / Evidence & reproducibilityTrace the result to its source

The standalone HTML embeds the measurement dataset, all eight vector figures, and byte-preserving primary result/calibration JSON files. Source download buttons decode the original bytes, so their SHA-256 values match this register. The companion evidence package also contains 300 dpi PNGs, SVGs, CSV tables, source hashes, and report-generation code. Other original logs and preservation receipts are represented by hashes and selected fields; the package is not a complete copy of every private machine log.

Rebuild: with Python, NumPy, matplotlib and Jinja2 available, run python build_publication.py inside the publication folder next to the original evidence root. The analysis module asserts the selected request counts, matches all 61 coding answers to their validation receipts, and checks identical RPC/native answer hashes before rendering. Rebuilding figures is offline report processing; it does not start model servers. A portable copy of every original input log is not included, so rebuilding from the companion package alone requires the retained source evidence tree. All displayed measurements and figures remain usable without it.

Supporting technical references

  • Captured source: llama-v1.0.0-source.zip, recorded hash in section 03; inspect src/llama-moe-cache.cpp and ggml/src/ggml-rpc/ggml-rpc.cpp for cache upload and remote-backend mechanisms. Source behavior motivates the RPC interpretation; it is not a substitute for an isolated network benchmark.
  • Microsoft: PrefetchVirtualMemory. Explains the Windows API involved in prefetching. These calls can affect system-wide file-cache pressure outside the process working-set accounting.
  • Pinned model configuration used in the conversion receipt. External URL is recorded provenance, not an assertion of present availability.

Bounded conclusion

For this model and these completed configurations, Strata remained the faster tested serving route. Native llama.cpp provided a functioning alternative and exposed useful cache/CPU-share controls, but its completed MTP pairs did not improve throughput. The distributed run demonstrated useful combined allocation and one correct answer; its relay-based, zero-CPU-share route was substantially slower than a single GPU. The uncompleted variants remain uncompleted, and no broader performance or coding-quality claim is inferred from them.

Prepared from the preserved 17 November 2026 experiment record. Report generation did not load models, rerun inference, modify serving profiles, or operate the desktop. The HTML embeds its figures and measurement dataset and works offline. Publication-grade presentation does not turn a limited field experiment into a controlled or peer-reviewed study.
